title: Magnetic Particle Inspection for Steel Mills | MPI (US)
description: Mag particle inspection for US steel mills and metals plants: ladle hooks, crane welds, shafts, gearboxes, rolls, caster frames. On-site MPI. Request a quote.
h1: Magnetic Particle Inspection for Steel Mills and Primary Metals Plants in the United States
html:
Magnetic particle inspection (MPI, or mag particle testing) is the fastest way to find fatigue and weld cracks on the steel parts that keep a mill running. Atlantis NDT inspects ladle hooks and trunnions, crane girders and wheels, shafts, gear and mill-stand components, caster frames and furnace structure at US steel and metals plants. Technicians are mobilized to your site. Send the component list and request an MT inspection quote.

Why steel plants use MPI so heavily

Almost everything that matters structurally in a steel plant is ferromagnetic carbon or alloy steel, which is exactly what magnetic particle testing is designed for. The loads are repetitive and large. A ladle hook sees the full weight of a heat each cycle, a crane girder flexes with every lift, a roll drive shaft transmits torque pulses, and a gearbox housing vibrates constantly. Cracks that begin at a surface notch, a weld toe or a sharp fillet grow in small steps, and a technician with a yoke and a can of particles can find them while they are still short. The result appears on the part itself, so the mill's maintenance engineer sees what the inspector saw.

MPI shows surface and near-surface cracks. It does not tell you how deep they go, and it does not look into a thick forging. Those jobs belong to ultrasonic testing for steel. Parts in aluminum, stainless steel and copper alloys are not magnetic, and the penetrant testing page for steel plants covers them.

What we examine, and why each part matters

  • Ladle hooks, trunnions and crane hooks. A crack in the hook saddle or shank can lead to a dropped ladle. MPI is applied to the full hook body and the thread area, with attention to stamped marks and sharp corners.
  • Crane girders, end trucks and wheels. Weld toes at diaphragms and stiffeners, bridge rail attachments, axle journals and wheel flanges. Our job page on magnetic particle inspection of lifting equipment goes into detail.
  • Shafts and spindles. Roll drive shafts, coupling hubs, pinion shafts and pump shafts, with the keyway and shoulder given particular attention.
  • Weldments. Mill housings, tundish and caster supports, platforms and runway beams. See magnetic particle weld inspection for the weld examination page.
  • Castings and forgings. Gear blanks, bearing housings, mill stand parts and pinions, with detailed acceptance notes on the page for castings and forgings.
  • Structural steel. Building frames and crane supports, covered by structural steel and bridge MPI.

Steel regions we work in

Atlantis has no office at any mill. Crews travel to the plant from the city that fits the schedule, and these pages carry the regional detail.

  • Magnetic particle testing in Gary for the northwest Indiana lakefront mills and coke works.

  • Magnetic particle testing in Pittsburgh for the Mon Valley mills and heavy fabricators.
  • Magnetic particle testing in Cleveland for northeast Ohio steel and the machine shops that serve it.
  • Magnetic particle testing in Toledo for northwest Ohio metals and automotive suppliers.

  • Magnetic particle testing in Buffalo for western New York forges and plate fabricators.
  • Magnetic particle testing in Birmingham for Alabama mills, foundries and pipe plants.

Standards that govern the examination

ASTM E709 is the guide for magnetic particle testing, and ASTM E1444 gives the practice. ASME Section V Article 7 is the reference when a code calls for MT, and ASTM A275 covers magnetic particle examination of steel forgings. ASTM A903 provides surface acceptance standards for steel castings. For cranes, OSHA 29 CFR 1910.179 requires inspection of overhead and gantry cranes in general industry, ASME B30.2 is the consensus standard, ASME B30.10 covers hooks, and AWS D14.1 governs welding of industrial and mill cranes. Acceptance criteria come from the owner, the crane or equipment maker, or the code the part was built to. We apply the named criterion and report; the decision to grind out, repair, derate or scrap belongs to the plant. Technicians work under the company written practice built on ASNT SNT-TC-1A, with Level II performing the test and an ASNT Level III approving procedures and signing reports. The code article is ASME Section V Article 7 explained.

Magnetizing methods for mill components

The direction of the magnetic field decides which cracks show. A crack is revealed when it crosses the field at a significant angle, so each area is magnetized in two directions.

  • Yoke. The standard field tool. An AC yoke is quick for weld toes and corners, and a lifting force check is done on the yoke as the procedure requires. Pole spacing is kept within the range the procedure sets.
  • Prods. Used on heavy weldments where more current is needed. Prods demand clean contact points to avoid arc burns on the part, so many plants restrict them and require a yoke.
  • Coil or cable wrap. For longer parts such as shafts and spindles, wrapping the part with a flexible cable magnetizes it along its length so transverse cracks show.
  • Central conductor or head shot. For parts removed from the stand and taken to a shop, passing current through the part reveals longitudinal cracks.

Particles can be dry powder, which tolerates warm surfaces better than liquid suspensions, or wet visible or fluorescent particles. Black particles on white contrast paint work well on dark weathered steel. Fluorescent work needs a darkened enclosure. The procedure states the choice and the surface temperature limit, and we check the part temperature before we start.

Surface and heat problems unique to mills

Mill scale, scaled hooks, grease and old paint hide cracks. We clean to bare metal in the inspection areas. Parts near furnaces and hot lines may be too hot for wet methods, so dry powder or a cool-down is used. Residual magnetism is another issue: shafts and bearing seats retain a field after testing, which attracts steel particles into bearings. We demagnetize rotating parts and record the check. Wind, spray from water cooling and conveyor dust also disturb particle patterns, so we use screens or choose the time of day.

Finds, misses and honest limits

MPI is strong for surface cracks and laps. It will not size depth, it will miss flaws more than a short distance below the surface, and it cannot examine austenitic stainless or aluminum. A thick coating or heavy rust reduces sensitivity. Atlantis does not perform radiography in the United States, and the specialist techniques outside MT, PT and UT are not part of this service.

A closer look at a ladle hook examination

A typical hook job shows how the pieces fit together. The hook is lowered to a platform or removed, and the full surface is cleaned to bare metal, including the threads of a shank nut if one is fitted. We check the hook against the maker's drawing for wear at the saddle and the throat opening, since a stretched throat is a visual finding and not an MPI one. Then the body is magnetized in two directions with a yoke, the saddle and shank-to-body transition get extra passes, and the stamped identification area is looked at because cold-stamped letters concentrate stress. Any indication is marked, photographed and measured. If the hook has been repaired by welding, the repair area is examined with the weld criteria and the plant's repair procedure. The report records the hook identification so each hook builds its own history, and a growing crack between outages becomes obvious from one report to the next.

Welded repairs and re-examination

Steel plants repair a great deal in place. A cracked crane girder weld is gouged out, rewelded and ground, and a torn bracket is replaced. MPI is used at two points: on the excavation, to confirm the whole crack is gone before welding begins, and on the finished weld after it has cooled to the temperature the welding procedure specifies for final examination. Some codes ask for a delay before final inspection on certain steels because hydrogen cracking can appear after welding. The delay is set by the code or the welding procedure and we follow it.

Plant access and outage planning

Mills control access closely. Contractors complete safety orientation, lock-out and tag-out under 29 CFR 1910.147, confined-space permits under 1910.146 where applicable, hot work permits, and fall protection on crane runways. Heat, noise and dust are normal. Crane inspections are normally done during a crane outage, with the crane parked and locked out and access by lift or platform. We agree dates with your planner and do not promise arrival times.

What the report contains

The report identifies each component and location, the procedure and revision, the equipment (yoke or coil, particle type, lift test and light levels), the surface condition and cleaning, the temperature, and the technician and level. Every indication is listed with position, length and orientation, photographed where possible, and judged against the named code. A Level III reviews and signs. Re-examination after repair uses the same format.

What to send for a quote

  • List of components with drawings, photographs and previous inspection records.
  • Material, surface condition and operating temperature of each part.
  • Acceptance code or owner or maker standard, and the crane or equipment rating where relevant.
  • Access, permits and the party supplying lifts and power.
  • Plant address, safety orientation requirements and the outage window.

Training your mill technicians

Mills that want routine crack checks done in-house can train staff through MT Level 1 training and MT Level 2 training, with practice on the magnetic particle simulator. The employer certifies under SNT-TC-1A, and a written practice sets the rules. For choosing between methods, see MT versus PT and the national magnetic particle testing page, and manufacturing NDT training for workforce programs.

faq.q: How often should ladle hooks be inspected with MPI?
faq.a: The interval comes from the crane maker, ASME B30.2 and B30.10 guidance, and the plant's own program, so we do not set it. We perform the examination you schedule and report indications against your criteria. Many plants combine MPI with UT at each scheduled crane outage.

faq.q: Can MPI be done on a hot hook or shaft?
faq.a: Only within the temperature limits in the procedure. Dry powder tolerates warmer surfaces than liquid suspensions, but very hot parts must cool or the test must wait for the outage. We measure surface temperature before starting and record it.

faq.q: Will magnetic particle testing find cracks under paint?
faq.a: Thin, well-bonded paint can be tested if the procedure has been shown to work through it, but thick paint, scale and rust reduce sensitivity. We ask for local cleaning at weld toes, pin bores and keyways so the examination is meaningful.

faq.q: Do you demagnetize shafts after testing?
faq.a: Yes, rotating parts and bearing seats are demagnetized when the procedure requires it, and the check is recorded in the report. A residual field attracts steel debris into bearings, so we treat this as part of the job.

faq.q: Is MPI acceptable for crane weld repairs under AWS D14.1?
faq.a: AWS D14.1 governs welding of industrial and mill cranes and sets the criteria usually applied to the examination. We follow the criterion named in your order or the crane maker's repair procedure, and report each indication against it.

faq.q: What can't magnetic particle testing find?
faq.a: It cannot examine non-magnetic metals such as stainless steel, aluminum and copper alloys, and it does not find flaws buried deep in thick sections or measure crack depth. For those cases we use penetrant testing or ultrasonic testing.

faq.q: What do you need from us to quote MPI at a mill?
faq.a: Send a component list with drawings or photographs, material and operating temperatures, the acceptance code, access and permit arrangements, plant safety orientation requirements and the outage window. We reply within one business day.

faq.q: Who decides whether a cracked part stays in service?
faq.a: You do, with your engineer and, for cranes, the owner's qualified person and the maker's guidance. Our report lists the indications against the named criterion. We do not make fitness-for-service or return-to-service decisions.

faq.q: Can you do radiographic inspection of mill welds?
faq.a: No. Atlantis does not perform radiography in the United States because it requires a radiation license. Owners hire a licensed contractor where radiography is specified, and we can review the films or images as an ASNT Level III service.
